claims.evidence: Supported by mSTARR-seq data comparing methylated and unmethylated conditions under IFNA stimulation

claims.claim: Methylation-dependent responses to IFNA identified via mSTARR-seq predict methylation-dependent transcriptional responses to challenge with influenza virus in human macrophages.
claims.source: In agreement, methylation-dependent responses to IFNA identified via mSTARR-seq predict methylation-dependent transcriptional responses to challenge with influenza virus in human macrophages.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of mSTARR-seq data with in vivo macrophage data from Aracena et al., 2024

claims.claim: Pre-existing DNA methylation patterns can influence the response to subsequent environmental exposures, supporting the biological embedding hypothesis.
claims.source: Our observations support the idea that pre-existing DNA methylation patterns can influence the response to subsequent environmental exposures—one of the tenets of biological embedding.
claims.evidence: Supported by mSTARR-seq data showing methylation-dependent responses to environmental challenges

claims.claim: Sites previously associated with early life adversity are not more likely to functionally influence gene regulation than expected by chance.
claims.source: However, we also find that, on average, sites previously associated with early life adversity are not more likely to functionally influence gene regulation than expected by chance.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of 27 early life adversity studies compared to mSTARR-seq regulatory activity data

claims.claim: DNA methylation is sensitive to the environment, can remain stable across cell divisions, and in some contexts, can alter gene regulation.
claims.source: DNA methylation is sensitive to the environment, can remain stable across cell divisions, and in some contexts, can alter gene regulation.
claims.evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus

claims.claim: DNA methylation has received high attention as a potential pathway linking environmental exposures to downstream trait variation, especially when exposures are temporally separated.
claims.source: Consequently, it has received a high level of attention as a potential pathway linking environmental exposures to downstream trait variation, especially when these exposures are separated temporally, as proposed by the 'biological embedding' hypothesis (Hertzman, 1999; Hertzman, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hertzman 1999 and 2012

claims.claim: Gestational manipulation of methyl donors in mice is causally implicated in changes in DNA methylation and expression levels of the agouti gene, which affects susceptibility to obesity and insulin resistance later in life.
claims.source: In a canonical example, gestational manipulation of methyl donors in mice is causally implicated in changes in DNA methylation and expression levels of the agouti gene, which in turn affects susceptibility to obesity and insulin resistance later in life (Dolinoy et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dolinoy et al., 2006

claims.claim: The mechanism underlying the agouti case—'metastable' methylation of an inserted intracisternal A particle [IAP] class retrovirus—is now thought to be unusual.
claims.source: However, the mechanism underlying the agouti case—'metastable' methylation of an inserted intracisternal A particle [IAP] class retrovirus—is now thought to be unusual (Kazachenka et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kazachenka et al., 2018

claims.claim: It remains unclear whether environment-DNA methylation associations represent links along a causal pathway to phenotype or are better viewed as passive biomarkers of exposure.
claims.source: Thus, it remains unclear whether the many reports of environment-DNA methylation associations are likely to represent links along a causal pathway to phenotype, or are better viewed as passive biomarkers of exposure.
claims.evidence: Represents a gap in knowledge that motivates the study

claims.claim: Transcription factor binding is frequently (but not ubiquitously) sensitive to DNA methylation.
claims.source: In vitro studies reveal that transcription factor binding is frequently (but not ubiquitously) sensitive to DNA methylation (O'Malley et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to O'Malley et al., 2016 and Yin et al., 2017

claims.claim: Epigenomic editing of DNA methylation marks has been shown to alter the activity of transcription factors important in disease and development in vivo.
claims.source: More recently, epigenomic editing of DNA methylation marks has been shown to alter the activity of transcription factors important in disease and development in vivo (Greenberg and Bourc'his, 2019; Yim et al., 2020), as well as the formation of CTCF-mediated gene loops (Lei et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Greenberg and Bourc'his, 2019; Yim et al., 2020; and Lei et al., 2017

claims.claim: Even within the same regulatory element, changes in DNA methylation have functional consequences for gene expression at only a subset of sites.
claims.source: However, other epigenetic editing studies show that, even within the same regulatory element, changes in DNA methylation have functional consequences for gene expression at only a subset of sites (e.g. Maeder et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Maeder et al., 2013

claims.claim: In the native genome, enhancer activity appears to be insensitive to DNA methylation levels in the majority of cases.
claims.source: Indeed, in the native genome, enhancer activity appears to be insensitive to DNA methylation levels in the majority of cases (Kreibich et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kreibich et al., 2023

claims.claim: In response to a pathogen challenge, nearly all changes in gene expression precede changes in DNA methylation in human dendritic cells.
claims.source: Time series analyses in human dendritic cells have also shown that, in response to a pathogen challenge, nearly all changes in gene expression precede changes in DNA methylation (Pacis et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pacis et al., 2019

claims.claim: Methylation changes after pathogen infection may be functionally relevant if they influence the speed and magnitude of subsequent challenges by marking the accessibility of latent enhancers across cell divisions.
claims.source: Such methylation changes may nevertheless be functionally relevant if they influence the speed and magnitude of subsequent challenges (e.g. by marking the accessibility of latent enhancers across cell divisions) (Kamada et al., 2018; Sun and Barreiro, 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kamada et al., 2018 and Sun and Barreiro, 2020

claims.claim: Enhanced transcriptional responses to glucocorticoid stimulation occur in the descendants of hippocampal progenitor cells previously challenged with glucocorticoids.
claims.source: This hypothesis may explain, for example, enhanced transcriptional responses to glucocorticoid stimulation in the descendants of hippocampal progenitor cells previously challenged with glucocorticoids (Provençal et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Provençal et al., 2020

claims.claim: Environment-associated DNA methylation marks are mixed sets that include functionally silent sites, sites that are constitutively important for gene regulation, and sites in which DNA methylation levels affect gene regulation only under certain conditions.
claims.source: Together, these findings suggest that environment-associated DNA methylation marks are mixed sets that include functionally silent sites, sites that are constitutively important for gene regulation, and sites in which DNA methylation levels affect gene regulation only under certain conditions.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the cited literature

claims.claim: The study assessed regulatory activity and methylation-dependent regulatory activity for 4,558,475 600-base pair windows of the genome.
claims.source: We assessed regulatory activity and methylation-dependent regulatory activity for 4,558,475 600-base pair windows of the genome by pairing hybridization capture of targeted loci in the human genome with the massively parallel reporter assay, mSTARR-seq (Lea et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Describes the experimental design and scale

claims.claim: mSTARR-seq performs enzymatic manipulation of DNA methylation across hundreds of thousands to millions of reporter DNA fragments simultaneously.
claims.source: In brief, mSTARR-seq performs enzymatic manipulation of DNA methylation across hundreds of thousands to millions of reporter DNA fragments simultaneously.
claims.evidence: Describes the technical capability of the method

claims.claim: mSTARR-seq generates estimates of the enhancer-like regulatory potential for each fragment when that fragment is in an unmethylated versus a methylated state.
claims.source: By measuring the ability of fragments to self-transcribe (as in Arnold et al., 2013; Shlyueva et al., 2014; reviewed in Gallego Romero and Lea, 2022), it generates estimates of the enhancer-like regulatory potential for each fragment when that fragment is in an unmethylated versus a methylated state (Figure 1A, B).
claims.evidence: Describes the method and references Figure 1A, B; supported by citations

claims.claim: The study targeted all CpG sites on the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC array and those likely to be profiled using reduced representation bisulfite sequencing.
claims.source: To focus on the CpG sites most likely to be included in DNA methylation studies in humans, we performed custom capture with SeqCap EZ Prime Choice Probes (Roche), targeting all CpG sites on the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC array and those likely to be profiled using reduced representation bisulfite sequencing, which enriches for CpG sites near targets of MspI restriction enzyme digestion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Describes experimental design; references Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: The study targeted the 6.5 Mb in and flanking NR3C1 due to substantial attention to potential environmental and early life effects on DNA methylation at the glucocorticoid receptor gene.
claims.source: Because of substantial attention to potential environmental and early life effects on DNA methylation at the glucocorticoid receptor gene (NR3C1, reviewed in Liu and Nusslock, 2018), we also targeted the 6.5 Mb in and flanking NR3C1.
claims.evidence: Describes experimental design rationale; supported by citation to Liu and Nusslock, 2018

claims.claim: The study targeted a control set of 100,000 loci chosen at random across the human genome to assess background expectations for regulatory and methylation-dependent regulatory activity.
claims.source: Finally, to assess background expectations for regulatory and methylation-dependent regulatory activity in the human genome, we targeted a control set of 100,000 loci for capture, chosen at random across the human genome after excluding centromeres, gaps, and uncalled bases in the hg38 genome.
claims.evidence: Describes experimental design

claims.claim: 90.2% of the human genome was included in the plasmid DNA library purified at the end of the mSTARR-seq experiment.
claims.source: Based on our minimal criteria for assessment (600 basepair windows where at least half of the plasmid-derived DNA samples had non-zero reads covering the window; see Materials and methods), 90.2% of the human genome was included in the plasmid DNA library purified at the end of the mSTARR-seq experiment (mean sequencing depth per replicate = 30.4 million reads; mean read coverage per window = 12.723 ± 41.696 s.d.).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequencing data analysis

claims.claim: Windows were ~15 fold enriched for targeted regions in the genome.
claims.source: Within this set, which also included off-target regions, windows were ~15 fold enriched for targeted regions in the genome (Fisher's Exact Test log2(OR) 95% confidence interval (CI)=3.971 [3.934, 4.009], p<1.0 x 10–300).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of sequencing data

claims.claim: The study successfully targeted 99.3% of CpG sites on the MethylationEPIC array and 99.4% of sites likely to be included in RRBS libraries.
claims.source: Thus, in windows that passed our minimal assessment criteria, we successfully targeted 99.3% of CpG sites on the MethylationEPIC array and 99.4% of sites likely to be included in RRBS libraries.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of captured regions

claims.claim: Read depth was not predicted by CpG density, indicating no systematic power differences in assessing methylation-dependent activity due to differences in CpG number per window.
claims.source: Across target sets, read depth was not predicted by CpG density, indicating no systematic power differences in assessing methylation-dependent activity due to differences in CpG number per window (R2=0.099, p=0.6852; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claims.claim: DNA methylation levels were substantially higher in the methylated condition samples than in the unmethylated samples at the end of the experiment.
claims.source: We confirmed that DNA methylation levels were substantially higher in the methylated condition samples than in the unmethylated samples, where methylation levels were near zero (mean methylated = 0.885, mean unmethylated = 0.066, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; unpaired t-test: t=–14.66, df = 15,124, p=2.39 x 10–10).
claims.evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data; references Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claims.claim: Small deviations from 0% and 100% methylation would reduce power to detect methylation-dependent activity, but should not incur false positive results.
claims.source: We note that the observed small deviations from 0% and 100% methylation would reduce our power to detect methylation-dependent activity, but should not incur false positive results.
claims.evidence: Inference about the impact of observed methylation levels on statistical power

claims.claim: Among the regions analyzed, 3721 windows (1.7%) showed evidence for regulatory activity, where the amount of RNA generated from a window significantly exceeded the amount of DNA input sequenced for the same window (FDR <1%).
claims.source: Among the regions analyzed here, 3721 windows (1.7%) showed evidence for regulatory activity, where the amount of RNA generated from a window significantly exceeded the amount of DNA input sequenced for the same window (FDR <1%; Supplementary files 3; 0.082% of all windows where DNA reads were obtained in at least half of our replicate samples).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of mSTARR-seq data

claims.claim: Sequencing depth does not appear to constrain the ability to detect regulatory regions, as rarefaction analyses suggest that increasing sequencing depth would add only a small number of additional regions with evidence of transcriptional activity.
claims.source: Sequencing depth does not appear to constrain the ability to detect regulatory regions, as rarefaction analyses suggest that increasing sequencing depth of RNA or DNA libraries would add only a small number of additional regions with any evidence of transcriptional activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by rarefaction analysis; references Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claims.claim: Among analyzed windows, DNA coverage per fragment explains minimal variance in mSTARR-seq enhancer activity (R2=0.029).
claims.source: Further, among analyzed windows, DNA coverage per fragment explains minimal variance in mSTARR-seq enhancer activity (R2=0.029, p<1.0 x 10–300).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claims.claim: Regions with regulatory activity were enriched for enhancers and active promoters annotated by the ENCODE Consortium for the K562 cell line.
claims.source: Regions with regulatory activity were enriched for enhancers and active promoters annotated by the ENCODE Consortium for the K562 cell line log2(OR)=0.584–3.337; all p<1 x 10–3; Figure 1C; Supplementary file 4 (The ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012; Ernst and Kellis, 2012)
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison with ENCODE annotations; references Figure 1C

claims.claim: Many promoters can show enhancer-like activity in STARR-seq-type assays, although some promoters will be missed.
claims.source: note that previous research has found that many promoters can show enhancer-like activity in STARR-seq-type assays, although some promoters will be missed (e.g. Klein et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Klein et al., 2020

claims.claim: Regulatory regions were highly consistent with previous mSTARR-seq data generated in K562 cells using a previously published, independently generated DNA library.
claims.source: In support of assay reproducibility, regulatory regions also were highly consistent with previous mSTARR-seq data generated in K562 cells using a previously published, independently generated DNA library that we reanalyzed using the current pipeline (overlap among windows with FDR <1% in each data set analyzed independently: log2(OR) [95% CI]=6.212 [6.086, 6.440], p<1.0 x 10–300; Figure 1—figure supplements 5-6; Supplementary files 5-6; Lea et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison with Lea et al., 2018 data; references Figure 1—figure supplements 5-6

claims.claim: Regions with mSTARR-seq-annotated regulatory activity exhibited a high degree of consistency between cell types.
claims.source: Regions with mSTARR-seq-annotated regulatory activity also exhibited a high degree of consistency between cell types.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison across K562, HepG2, and A549 cell lines

claims.claim: Regulatory regions detected in K562 cells were enriched among regulatory regions detected in HepG2 cells (log2(OR) [95% CI]=3.534 [3.381, 3.684], p=5.21 x 10–307).
claims.source: In a comparison against newly generated mSTARR-seq data from the HepG2 liver cell line, using the same mSTARR-seq library as in the previously published K562 experiments (Lea et al., 2018), regulatory regions detected in this study were enriched among regulatory regions detected in HepG2 cells (log2(OR) [95% CI]=3.534 [3.381, 3.684], p=5.21 x 10–307; Figure 1—figure supplements 5 and 7; Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison with HepG2 data; references Figure 1—figure supplements 5 and 7

claims.claim: Regulatory regions identified in K562 cells overlap with regulatory regions identified in a conventional STARR-seq experiment in A549 lung epithelial cells (log2(OR) [95% CI]=2.451 [2.442, 2.461], p<1.0 x 10–300).
claims.source: They also overlap with regulatory regions identified in a conventional STARR-seq experiment in A549 lung epithelial cells (log2(OR) [95% CI]=2.451 [2.442, 2.461], p<1.0 x 10–300) (Johnson et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison with Johnson et al., 2018 data

claims.claim: The findings can be generalized, to some extent, to other cell and tissue types beyond blood-derived cell lines.
claims.source: Although we prioritized a blood-derived cell line because of the frequency of environmental epigenetic studies done in blood, these results suggest that our findings can be generalized, to some extent, to other cell and tissue types.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from cross-cell type comparisons

claims.claim: Among the 3721 windows with regulatory activity in either the methylated or unmethylated condition, 1768 windows (47.5%) were differentially active depending on condition, pointing to DNA methylation-dependent regulatory activity.
claims.source: Among the 3721 windows with regulatory activity in either the methylated or unmethylated condition, 1768 windows (47.5% of regulatory windows; FDR <1%) were differentially active depending on condition, pointing to DNA methylation-dependent regulatory activity.
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of mSTARR-seq data

claims.claim: Effects of DNA methylation on regulatory activity in K562 cells are concordant with previously published K562 data and new HepG2 data.
claims.source: This result is also concordant when we apply the current pipeline to previously published data from K562s and our new HepG2 data, which exhibit correlated effects of DNA methylation on regulatory activity in the windows examined in both cases (K562: R2=0.286 for 1250 regulatory windows with FDR <1% in both data sets, p=3.19 x 10–93; HepG2: R2=0.277 for 511 regulatory windows with FDR <1% in both data sets, p=8.87 x 10–38 Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis; references Figure 1—figure supplement 8

claims.claim: Among methylation-dependent regulatory regions, the majority of regions (1744 windows, 98.6%) were more active in the unmethylated condition than the methylated condition.
claims.source: Among methylation-dependent regulatory regions, the majority of regions (1744 windows, 98.6%) were more active in the unmethylated condition than the methylated condition (Figure 1—figure supplements 9 and 10).
claims.evidence: Supported by mSTARR-seq data; references Figure 1—figure supplements 9 and 10

claims.claim: Regulatory regions with more CpGs are more likely to be repressed by DNA methylation (Spearman's rho = 0.370, p=9.865 x 10–121).
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings (Lea et al., 2018), regulatory regions with more CpGs are more likely to be repressed by DNA methylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 11; Spearman's rho = 0.370, p=9.865 x 10–121; n=3,721 regions with mSTARR-seq regulatory activity).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis; references Figure 1—figure supplement 11

claims.claim: Regulatory windows showing higher activity in the methylated condition (24 windows) were enriched for binding motifs of the transcription factor p53.
claims.source: Regulatory windows showing higher activity in the methylated condition (24 windows) were enriched for binding motifs of the transcription factors p53, which has been previously reported to have increased binding affinity to methylated DNA relative to unmethylated DNA (Kribelbauer et al., 2017) (log2(OR) [95% CI]=2.352 [0.714, 3.767], p=2.91 x 10–3; Supplementary file 8)
claims.evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis and citation to Kribelbauer et al., 2017

claims.claim: Regulatory windows showing higher activity in the methylated condition were enriched for binding motifs of Tfcp2I1, which has been found to recruit Tet2 to mediate enhancer demethylation.
claims.source: and Tfcp2I1, which has been found to recruit Tet2 to mediate enhancer demethylation (Sardina et al., 2018) (log2(OR) [95% CI]=2.615 [0.580, 4.229], p=6.84 x 10–3).
claims.evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis and citation to Sardina et al., 2018

claims.claim: Windows containing EPIC CpG sites, RRBS-associated sites, or located in or near NR3C1 were significantly more likely to show at least some degree of transcriptional activity than the genomic background.
claims.source: As expected, windows that contained EPIC CpG sites, sites associated with RRBS, or that were located in or near NR3C1 were significantly more likely to show at least some degree of transcriptional activity (i.e. show plasmid-derived RNA reads in at least half the sham or methylated replicates) than the genomic background (i.e. 98,967 randomly distributed loci: see Materials and Methods), and thus were more likely to be included in our analysis set (n=216,091 windows) for regulatory activity (EPIC: log2(OR) [95% CI]=2.189 [2.152, 2.227], p<1.0 x 10–300; RRBS: log2(OR) [95% CI]=4.126 [4.086, 4.163], p<1.0 x 10–300; NR3C1: log2(OR) [95% CI]=3.259 [3.193, 3.325], p<1.0 x 10–300; Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis; references Figure 1D

claims.claim: Windows containing EPIC array sites were not more likely to exhibit significant enhancer-like regulatory activity than background windows of the genome, conditional on minimal transcriptional activity.
claims.source: However, conditional on minimal transcriptional activity, windows containing EPIC array sites were not more likely to exhibit significant enhancer-like regulatory activity (FDR <1%; n=3721 windows) than background windows of the genome, and RRBS- and NR3C1-associated sites were in fact slightly less likely to do so (EPIC: log2(OR) [95% CI]=0.112 [-0.168, 0.405], p=0.47; RRBS: log2(OR) [95% CI]=−0.493 [-0.779,–0.195], p = 1.11 x 10–3; NR3C1: log2(OR) [95% CI]=−0.730 [-1.263,–0.217], p = 3.89 x 10–3).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claims.claim: Among regions with detectable regulatory activity, 63.3% of those containing RRBS-associated CpG sites exhibited methylation-dependent regulatory activity, compared to 45.9% of control background loci.
claims.source: In contrast, among regions with detectable regulatory activity, 63.3% of those containing RRBS-associated CpG sites exhibited methylation-dependent regulatory activity, compared to 45.9% of control background loci (RRBS against control: log2(OR) [95% CI]=1.025 [0.430, 1.624], p=4.39 x 10–4; Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis; references Figure 1D

claims.claim: Of 109 regulatory windows in the control set, 108 contain at least 1 CpG, so the difference in methylation-dependent activity is not because the control set is CpG-free.
claims.source: Note that of 109 regulatory windows in the control set, 108 contain at least 1 CpG, so this difference is not because the control set is CpG-free (mean number CpGs per fragment in control set = 13.291 ± 11.179 s.d.; EPIC = 19.641 ± 14.471; RRBS = 20.870 ± 13.883; NR3C1=7.405 ± 9.409).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of CpG content

claims.claim: Differential methylation identified through RRBS is more likely to be capable of driving differences in gene regulation, as detectable by mSTARR-seq, than differential methylation elsewhere in the genome.
claims.source: Consequently, differential methylation identified through RRBS is more likely to be capable of driving differences in gene regulation, as detectable by mSTARR-seq, than differential methylation elsewhere in the genome.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the enrichment of methylation-dependent activity in RRBS sites

claims.claim: 98.8% of RRBS sites do not occur in regions of the genome with detectable regulatory activity in either the methylated or unmethylated conditions, at least in the K562 cell type.
claims.source: We caution, however, that even among RRBS sites, 98.8% do not occur in regions of the genome with detectable regulatory activity in either the methylated or unmethylated conditions, at least in the K562 cell type, and 35.0% of those that fall in putative regulatory elements exhibit no evidence for methylation-dependent activity.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of RRBS sites

claims.claim: 35.0% of RRBS sites that fall in putative regulatory elements exhibit no evidence for methylation-dependent activity.
claims.source: We caution, however, that even among RRBS sites, 98.8% do not occur in regions of the genome with detectable regulatory activity in either the methylated or unmethylated conditions, at least in the K562 cell type, and 35.0% of those that fall in putative regulatory elements exhibit no evidence for methylation-dependent activity.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of RRBS sites

claims.claim: Enhancer activity can be cell type- or environment-dependent.
claims.source: Enhancer activity can be cell type- or environment-dependent (e.g. Ostuni et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2018; Chaudhri et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ostuni et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2018; Chaudhri et al., 2020

claims.claim: DNA methylation-dependent enhancer activity may show context-dependence similar to enhancer activity.
claims.source: DNA methylation-dependent enhancer activity may show similar context-dependence, thus potentially accounting for the large number of sites that fall in functionally silent regions described above.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on known properties of enhancer activity

claims.claim: Regions that were identified to have regulatory potential in the baseline condition were highly likely to retain regulatory potential after cells were challenged with IFNA or dex.
claims.source: Regions that were identified to have regulatory potential in the baseline condition were highly likely to retain regulatory potential after cells were challenged with IFNA or dex (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; IFNA log2(OR) [95% CI]=8.639 [8.499, 8.812], p<1.0 x 10–300; dex log2(OR) [95% CI]=9.640 [9.483, 9.776], p<1.0 x 10–323; Supplementary files 10-11).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison across conditions; references Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claims.claim: Environmental challenges revealed thousands of putative regulatory regions that were undetectable at baseline but active post-stimulation.
claims.source: However, environmental challenges also revealed thousands of putative regulatory regions that were undetectable at baseline but active post-stimulation (Figure 2B; 1614 IFNA-specific; 1131 dex-specific).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of regulatory activity across conditions; references Figure 2B

claims.claim: Of 4632 IFNA regulatory regions (<1% FDR), 44.1% are not detectable at baseline at a 1% FDR threshold, and 25.1% remain undetectable with a relaxed baseline FDR of 10%.
claims.source: Of 4632 IFNA regulatory regions (<1% FDR), 44.1% are not detectable at baseline at a 1% FDR threshold in the baseline condition, and even with a relaxed baseline FDR of 10%, 25.1% remain undetectable.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of regulatory activity across conditions

claims.claim: Of 4217 dex regulatory regions (<1% FDR), 40.2% are not detectable at baseline (1% FDR), and 31.5% remain undetectable at a baseline FDR of 10%.
claims.source: Of 4217 dex regulatory regions (<1% FDR), 40.2% are not detectable at baseline (1% FDR), and 31.5% remain undetectable at a baseline FDR of 10%.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of regulatory activity across conditions

claims.claim: The most enriched motif in IFNA-specific regulatory windows was the canonical DNA target of interferon signaling, known as IFN-stimulated response elements (ISRE).
claims.source: For example, the most enriched motif was the canonical DNA target of interferon signaling, known as IFN-stimulated response elements (ISRE; log2(OR) [95% CI]=3.158 [2.953, 3.358], Bonferroni corrected p=7.31 x 10–133), followed by binding motifs for several IFN-regulatory factors (IRF1, IRF2, IRF3, IRF4, IRF8; all OR >1.5 and Bonferroni corrected p<1 x 10–15; Chen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis

claims.claim: IFNA-specific regulatory windows were enriched for binding motifs for several IFN-regulatory factors (IRF1, IRF2, IRF3, IRF4, IRF8; all OR >1.5 and Bonferroni corrected p<1 x 10–15).
claims.source: For example, the most enriched motif was the canonical DNA target of interferon signaling, known as IFN-stimulated response elements (ISRE; log2(OR) [95% CI]=3.158 [2.953, 3.358], Bonferroni corrected p=7.31 x 10–133), followed by binding motifs for several IFN-regulatory factors (IRF1, IRF2, IRF3, IRF4, IRF8; all OR >1.5 and Bonferroni corrected p<1 x 10–15; Chen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis and citation to Chen et al., 2017

claims.claim: Regulatory windows specific to the dex-stimulated condition were significantly enriched for 28 transcription factor binding motifs.
claims.source: Regulatory windows specific to the dex-stimulated condition were significantly enriched for 28 transcription factor binding motifs, including the glucocorticoid response element IR3 and binding motifs of several transcription factors known to interact with or be modulated by the glucocorticoid receptor (AP-1, CEBP:CEBP, CEBP:AP1, JunB, Jun-AP1, GATA1, STAT3, and STAT5; all OR >1.3, Bonferroni corrected p<0.01; Supplementary file 13; Cain and Cidlowski, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis and citation to Cain and Cidlowski, 2017

claims.claim: Expressed genes located closest to mSTARR-seq-annotated, IFNA-specific enhancers were more strongly upregulated after IFNA stimulation than genes located closest to shared mSTARR-seq-annotated enhancers.
claims.source: These data showed that expressed genes located closest to mSTARR-seq-annotated, IFNA-specific enhancers were more strongly upregulated after IFNA stimulation than the set of expressed genes located closest to shared mSTARR-seq-annotated enhancers (i.e. those identified in both the IFNA and at least one other condition, considering genes within 100 kb maximum distance from each enhancer element; unpaired t-test; t=3.268, df = 601.88, p=1.15 x 10–3).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of endogenous gene expression data

claims.claim: Using inferred enhancer-gene linkages from EnhancerAtlas 2.0 and restricting to IFNA-specific enhancers with external experimental support for ISRE binding, genes near these enhancers were more strongly upregulated after IFNA stimulation (unpaired t-test; t=3.579, df = 118.36, p=5.01 x 10–4).
claims.source: We found similar results when using inferred enhancer-gene linkages from the EnhancerAtlas 2.0 (Gao et al., 2016) and restricting the set of IFNA-specific enhancers to those with external experimental support for ISRE binding (n=1005 windows; ChIP-Seq data from The ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012, relative to all other genes in the gene expression dataset; unpaired t-test; t=3.579, df = 118.36, p=5.01 x 10–4; Figure 2D; Supplementary file 16).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of endogenous gene expression data; references Figure 2D

claims.claim: Genes closest to dex-specific mSTARR-seq enhancers were more strongly upregulated after dex stimulation than genes near shared enhancers (unpaired t-test; t=3.477, df = 479.6, p=5.53 x 10–4).
claims.source: Despite a weaker overall gene expression response to dex, genes closest to dex-specific mSTARR-seq enhancers were also more strongly upregulated after dex stimulation than genes near shared enhancers (unpaired t-test; t=3.477, df = 479.6, p=5.53 x 10–4).

results.result: The authors applied mSTARR-seq to query nearly the entire human genome, assessing regulatory activity and methylation-dependent regulatory activity for 4,558,475 600-base pair windows. The study successfully targeted 99.3% of CpG sites on the MethylationEPIC array and 99.4% of sites likely to be included in RRBS libraries, with 90.2% of the human genome included in the plasmid DNA library.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C22-C30 collectively describe the experimental design, scope, and technical success of the mSTARR-seq approach. The data demonstrate comprehensive genome coverage with high capture efficiency for targeted CpG sites, supported by sequencing depth statistics and enrichment analyses (C28-C30). The technical reproducibility is validated by comparison with prior work (C1).

results.result: DNA methylation levels were substantially higher in the methylated condition samples (mean = 0.885) than in the unmethylated samples (mean = 0.066) at the end of the experiment, with read depth not predicted by CpG density.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 demonstrate successful experimental manipulation of DNA methylation status, validated by bisulfite sequencing (C32). The authors appropriately note that small deviations from complete methylation would reduce power but not cause false positives (C33), and show no systematic bias related to CpG density (C31).

results.result: Among the regions analyzed, 3,721 windows (1.7%) showed evidence for regulatory activity (FDR <1%), with sequencing depth appearing sufficient based on rarefaction analyses and minimal variance explained by DNA coverage per fragment (R²=0.029).
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 establish the identification of regulatory regions with appropriate statistical thresholds and quality controls. Rarefaction analysis (C35) validates sequencing depth sufficiency, and the minimal contribution of DNA coverage to variance (C36) indicates robust detection of regulatory activity independent of technical artifacts.

results.result: Regions with regulatory activity were enriched for ENCODE-annotated enhancers and active promoters in K562 cells and showed high consistency with previous mSTARR-seq data in K562 cells, HepG2 cells, and conventional STARR-seq in A549 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 validate the mSTARR-seq approach through multiple lines of evidence: enrichment in known regulatory elements (C37), consistency with prior independent experiments (C39), and cross-cell-type validation (C40-C42). The statistical support is strong (all p<1.0 x 10⁻³⁰⁰ for overlaps), demonstrating reproducibility and generalizability.

results.result: Among 3,721 windows with regulatory activity, 1,768 windows (47.5%) exhibited methylation-dependent regulatory activity (FDR <1%), with 98.6% showing higher activity in the unmethylated condition. Regulatory regions with more CpGs are more likely to be repressed by DNA methylation (Spearman's rho = 0.370).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 establish widespread methylation-dependent regulatory activity with strong statistical support. The concordance across K562 and HepG2 datasets (C45: R²=0.286 and 0.277) validates reproducibility. The relationship between CpG density and methylation repression (C47) is consistent with prior findings and mechanistically plausible.

results.result: Regulatory windows showing higher activity in the methylated condition (24 windows) were enriched for binding motifs of transcription factors p53 and Tfcp2I1, which have known interactions with methylated DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 identify a small subset of regions with increased activity when methylated, with enrichment for TF motifs known to preferentially bind methylated DNA (p53) or recruit demethylation machinery (Tfcp2I1). The findings are supported by motif enrichment analysis and consistent with prior literature on these TFs.

results.result: Windows containing RRBS-associated CpG sites showed enrichment for methylation-dependent regulatory activity (63.3% vs 45.9% in controls), but 98.8% of RRBS sites do not occur in regions with detectable regulatory activity in K562 cells, and 35.0% of those in regulatory elements show no methylation-dependent activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 demonstrate that while RRBS sites are enriched for methylation-dependent regulatory activity relative to background (C52), the vast majority of RRBS sites lack detectable regulatory function in this cell type (C55-C56). This is a critical finding that challenges assumptions about the functional relevance of commonly studied methylation sites, though the authors appropriately note cell-type specificity as a caveat.

results.result: Environmental challenges with IFNA or dexamethasone revealed thousands of putative regulatory regions undetectable at baseline (1,614 IFNA-specific; 1,131 dex-specific), with 44.1% of IFNA regulatory regions and 40.2% of dex regulatory regions not detectable at baseline (1% FDR).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 demonstrate context-dependent regulatory activity, with environmental stimulation revealing cryptic regulatory elements. The statistical support is strong (C59: log2(OR) >8.5, p<1.0 x 10⁻³⁰⁰), and the findings are consistent with known biology of enhancer context-dependence (C57). The substantial proportion of condition-specific elements (C61-C62) represents a major finding about the limitations of baseline-only regulatory assays.

results.result: IFNA-specific regulatory windows were enriched for ISRE motifs and IRF binding motifs, while dex-specific windows were enriched for glucocorticoid response elements and binding motifs of GR-interacting transcription factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 validate the biological relevance of condition-specific regulatory regions through enrichment of expected transcription factor binding motifs. The enrichments are highly significant (Bonferroni corrected p<0.01) and mechanistically consistent with known signaling pathways for IFNA and dexamethasone responses.

results.result: Genes located closest to condition-specific mSTARR-seq enhancers showed stronger upregulation after the corresponding stimulation than genes near shared enhancers, for both IFNA (t=3.579, p=5.01 x 10⁻⁴) and dex (t=3.477, p=5.53 x 10⁻⁴) conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 demonstrate that condition-specific regulatory activity detected by mSTARR-seq predicts endogenous gene expression responses. The statistical support is adequate (p<0.001 for both conditions), and the use of enhancer-gene linkages from EnhancerAtlas 2.0 (C68) provides additional validation. This connects the reporter assay findings to native genomic function.

results.result: DNA methylation state plays an important role in shaping IFNA-specific responses, with 81.4% of IFNA-specific regulatory windows exhibiting methylation-dependent activity. Windows with ISRE binding support show strong methylation-dependence after IFNA stimulation (t=31.748, p=1.02 x 10⁻¹⁵³) but not at baseline.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 establish widespread DNA methylation-environment interactions for IFNA response. The statistical support is exceptionally strong (C71: p=3.58 x 10⁻³¹²; C75: p=1.02 x 10⁻¹⁵³), and the finding that 99.8% of methylation-dependent windows with interferon TF motifs are more active when unmethylated (C73) demonstrates a clear mechanistic pattern. This represents a major discovery about epigenetic priming.

results.result: In human macrophages, baseline DNA methylation at IFNA-specific mSTARR-seq enhancers predicts gene expression responses to influenza infection, with the correlation 3.44-fold stronger in IFNA-specific enhancers than shared enhancers. One enhancer at the ISG15 promoter explains 38% of variance in ISG15 response to flu across individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 provide critical in vivo validation of the mSTARR-seq findings using independent human macrophage data (n=35 individuals). The within-individual correlations are statistically significant (C79: all Bonferroni-corrected p<2 x 10⁻⁵), and the ISG15 example (C81-C83) demonstrates a large effect size (R²=0.38) at a biologically important gene. The similarity between IFNA and flu responses (C78) supports the relevance of the comparison.

results.result: ISG15 plays critical roles in regulating the type I interferon response and modulating host immunity to viral and bacterial infections.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 provides biological context for the ISG15 finding, supported by citation to a review (Perng and Lenschow, 2018). This establishes the functional importance of the identified methylation-dependent regulatory element.

results.result: For 26 of 27 early life adversity studies, ELA-associated CpG sites were not more likely to occur within putative regulatory windows than background chance. The exception (Cao-Lei et al., 2014) showed enrichment for regulatory potential but not for methylation-dependent activity, likely due to its focus on intermediately methylated, variable CpG sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 demonstrate that most ELA-associated sites lack detectable regulatory function in K562 cells. The statistical analyses are appropriate (Fisher's exact tests), and the authors provide a plausible explanation for the single exception (C91-C92). However, the limitation to K562 cells and specific environmental conditions (acknowledged in C87) means this finding may not generalize to all relevant cell types and contexts.

results.result: DNA methylation often significantly attenuates regulatory activity in K562 enhancer and promoter elements, but 98% of CpG sites associated with early life adversity fell in windows with no discernible regulatory potential in K562 cells, suggesting many ELA-associated sites may be passive biomarkers rather than causal links.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 synthesize the findings on methylation-dependent regulation and ELA sites. The high rate of methylation-dependence (47.5% from C44) supports C93, and the lack of regulatory activity at most ELA sites (C94) supports the biomarker interpretation (C95). However, the inference in C95 is limited by the use of a single cell type and may not apply to other relevant tissues.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that other cell types and cellular contexts should be tested to further evaluate the ELA hypothesis, noting that the relationship between glucocorticoid signaling and early life adversity is complex and may not be well-modeled by acute exposure. Expanding mSTARR-seq to other contexts can help prioritize CpG sites from observational studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 appropriately acknowledge limitations and suggest future directions. The authors recognize that K562 cells may not be the most relevant model for all ELA effects (C96), that acute dex exposure may not capture chronic stress effects (C97), and that enhancer repertoires differ across cell types (C98). These are reasonable caveats that temper the interpretation of the ELA findings.

results.result: DNA methylation-environment interactions are widespread in the human genome, with regulatory activity and methylation-dependent effects often only detectable upon stimulation. IFNA-specific enhancers can identify loci where baseline DNA methylation predicts gene expression responses to flu infection, with the ISG15 effect accounting for over a third of variance in the fold-change response.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C106 synthesize the major findings on methylation-environment interactions. The widespread nature of these interactions (C101-C102) is supported by the data showing thousands of condition-specific regulatory regions (C60-C62) and high rates of methylation-dependence in IFNA-specific elements (C71). The in vivo validation (C103) and large effect size at ISG15 (C105) strengthen the biological relevance of these findings.

results.result: The authors conclude that while many DNA methylation differences are functionally silent, the functional importance of DNA methylation is likely underestimated without considering its interaction with the cellular environment. Future applications of mSTARR-seq in additional cell types may help resolve questions about trained immunity and repeated challenge responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 provide a balanced synthesis of the findings. The conclusion that many methylation differences are silent (C108) is supported by the ELA analysis and prior literature, while the importance of environmental context (C109) is strongly supported by the condition-specific regulatory activity data (C60-C62, C71). The suggestion for future work (C107) is reasonable and well-motivated.

results.result: The authors applied mSTARR-seq to assess regulatory activity and methylation-dependent regulatory activity for 4,558,475 600-base pair windows across nearly the entire human genome, targeting CpG sites from the Illumina EPIC array, RRBS, the NR3C1 gene region, and random control sites.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge the scope and scale of the study. Reviewer 3 states 'The scope of this study is very impressive' and Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'provide a great resource of DNA methylation sensitive enhancers.' The editor describes the work as using 'a genome-wide, massively parallel reporter assay,' affirming the experimental design and coverage.

results.result: The mSTARR-seq experiment successfully captured 90.2% of the human genome in the plasmid library, with ~15-fold enrichment for targeted regions, achieving 99.3% coverage of EPIC array CpG sites and 99.4% of RRBS sites. DNA methylation levels were substantially higher in methylated samples (mean=0.885) than unmethylated samples (mean=0.066).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the technical success of the capture or methylation manipulation. Reviewer 3 notes 'the method utilized is currently the best method to do so,' implicitly accepting the technical execution. No concerns are raised about coverage or methylation efficiency.

results.result: Among analyzed regions, 3,721 windows (1.7%) showed evidence for regulatory activity (FDR <1%). These regions were enriched for ENCODE-annotated enhancers and promoters, showed high consistency with previous mSTARR-seq data in K562 cells, and exhibited cross-cell-type consistency with HepG2 and A549 cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the identification of regulatory regions. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'validate their baseline findings using additional datasets, including RNAseq data and show convergences across two cell lines.' The editor notes the authors 'provide compelling evidence' for their findings. No concerns are raised about the regulatory activity detection.

results.result: Among regulatory windows, 1,768 (47.5%) exhibited methylation-dependent regulatory activity (FDR <1%), with 98.6% showing higher activity when unmethylated. Regions with more CpGs were more likely to be repressed by methylation (Spearman's rho=0.370). The minority of windows more active when methylated were enriched for p53 and Tfcp2l1 binding motifs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings. The editor states the authors 'provide compelling evidence that methylation not only influences baseline activity of regulatory sequences.' Reviewer 3 notes 'a relatively large fraction of these show an effect of methylation on expression.' No critiques of the methylation-dependence findings are raised.

results.result: Windows containing EPIC, RRBS, or NR3C1 sites were more likely to show transcriptional activity than genomic background, but conditional on minimal activity, only RRBS sites showed enrichment for methylation-dependent regulatory activity (63.3% vs. 45.9% in controls). However, 98.8% of RRBS sites showed no detectable regulatory activity, and 35.0% of those in regulatory elements showed no methylation-dependence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors provide a great resource of DNA methylation sensitive enhancers...given the focus on sites included in RBSS and the Illumina EPIC array.' The nuanced finding that most sites lack regulatory activity is not challenged.

results.result: Environmental challenges (IFNA and dexamethasone) revealed thousands of condition-specific regulatory regions undetectable at baseline (1,614 IFNA-specific, 1,131 dex-specific). IFNA-specific regions were enriched for ISRE and IRF motifs, while dex-specific regions were enriched for glucocorticoid response elements. Genes near condition-specific enhancers showed stronger upregulation after stimulation than genes near shared enhancers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the environmental response findings. Reviewer 1 states 'DNA methylation can influence changes in regulatory activity following a specific stimulation, even in absence of baseline effects.' The editor notes the authors show methylation affects 'the magnitude of acute responses to environmental stimuli.' No concerns are raised about the condition-specific regulatory regions.

results.result: For IFNA challenge, DNA methylation state played a critical role: 81.4% of IFNA-specific regulatory windows exhibited methylation-dependent activity (vs. 47.5% at baseline). Regions with interferon response motifs (ISRE, IRF1-8) strongly responded to IFNA when unmethylated but showed attenuated responses when methylated. Windows with ISRE binding showed no methylation-dependence at baseline but strong dependence after IFNA stimulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support these findings. Reviewer 1 states this is 'very convincingly shown for INFA response sequences.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'are able to report several important findings, including that pre-existing DNA methylation patterns can influence the response to subsequent environmental exposures.' The editor highlights this as 'compelling evidence.'

results.result: Methylation-dependent responses to IFNA identified via mSTARR-seq predicted methylation-dependent transcriptional responses to influenza virus challenge in human macrophages. Within individuals, baseline DNA methylation at IFNA-specific mSTARR-seq enhancers negatively correlated with gene expression responses to flu (mean r=-0.170), with correlation 2.44 times stronger after infection than at baseline. One enhancer at the ISG15 promoter showed methylation explaining 38% of variance in ISG15 response to flu.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm the in vivo validation. Reviewer 1 states 'This is very convincingly shown for INFA response sequences, where baseline methylation is predictive of the transcriptional response to flu infection in human macrophages.' The editor notes the findings are 'compelling.' No concerns are raised about the macrophage validation data.

results.result: The findings support the biological embedding hypothesis: pre-existing DNA methylation patterns can influence responses to subsequent environmental exposures. DNA methylation-environment interactions are widespread, with regulatory activity and methylation-dependent effects often only detectable upon stimulation, consistent with DNA methylation contributing to epigenomic priming.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this interpretation. Reviewer 1 states the data 'lends support that difference in DNA methylation can alter responses to environmental stimuli and thus of the possibility that environmental exposures that alter DNS methylation can also alter subsequent response to this exposure, in line with the theory of epigenetic embedding.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors report 'pre-existing DNA methylation patterns can influence the response to subsequent environmental exposures.'

results.result: Sites previously associated with early life adversity (ELA) from 27 studies were not more likely to occur in regulatory windows than expected by chance (26 of 27 studies showed no enrichment). 98% of ELA-associated CpG sites fell in windows with no discernible regulatory potential in K562 cells. The exception was Cao-Lei et al. 2014, which showed enrichment likely due to focus on intermediately methylated, variable sites.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 initially raised concerns that 'this approach does not seem an optimal model to explore this relationship in vivo' because 'exposure to early adversity and its consequences is not directly correlated with glucocorticoid release.' After revision, Reviewer 1 states 'the authors have now discussed this issue carefully, so that this point is addressed,' but does not explicitly endorse the conclusion. The interpretation remains qualified by cell-type and context limitations acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations: other cell types and cellular contexts should be tested to further evaluate whether ELA-associated sites are passive biomarkers. The relationship between glucocorticoid signaling and early life adversity is complex and may not be well-modeled by acute glucocorticoid exposure. The repertoire of active enhancers differs across cell types and states, so expanding mSTARR-seq to other contexts could help prioritize CpG sites from observational studies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these caveats. Reviewer 1 notes that after revision 'the authors have now discussed this issue carefully' regarding the limitations of the dex model for ELA. The acknowledgment of cell-type specificity and need for additional contexts is consistent with reviewer concerns and is not challenged.

results.result: DNA methylation often significantly attenuates regulatory activity in K562 enhancer and promoter elements. The findings dovetail with work supporting the importance of CpG sites within enhancers in responding to environmental perturbations. mSTARR-seq could help identify additional in vivo DNA methylation-environment interactions and resolve questions about trained immunity and repeated challenge responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the broader implications. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provide a great resource' that 'can now be used for functional interpretation of large scale datasets.' The editor notes 'the extensive data set will likely become a key resource for the community.' Reviewer 3 states 'I am certain that these data will become an important resource for the community.'

High agreement on study design validation.

Strong agreement on regulatory activity detection.

OpenEval provides specific correlation coefficients and CpG density relationships, while peer reviewers affirm that methylation influences baseline activity and note the large fraction showing methylation effects. Strong agreement.

Complete agreement with appropriate caveats about cell-type specificity.

Strong agreement on environmental context importance.

Both strongly support widespread methylation-environment interactions for IFNA response (C70-C76). OpenEval provides exceptional statistical support and mechanistic patterns, while peer reviewers describe this as 'very convincingly shown' and 'compelling evidence.' Complete agreement on this major discovery.

Both strongly support in vivo validation using human macrophage data (C77-C83). OpenEval details within-individual correlations and ISG15 effect size, while peer reviewers describe this as 'very convincingly shown' with baseline methylation predicting flu response. Complete agreement on validation strength.

Both address ELA-associated sites lacking regulatory function (C86-C92), but with different confidence levels. OpenEval finds claims supported with appropriate caveats about cell-type limitations. Peer reviewers initially raised concerns about the dex model for ELA, marking this as UNCERTAIN even after revisions addressed the issue. Partial agreement with acknowledged limitations.

Both address interpretation of ELA findings (C93-C95). OpenEval supports the biomarker interpretation with caveats about single cell type limitations. Peer reviewers remain UNCERTAIN about the ELA conclusions despite acknowledging careful discussion of limitations. Agreement on data but divergence on strength of interpretation.

Both support the acknowledgment of limitations (C96-C99). OpenEval finds these caveats appropriate and reasonable, while peer reviewers accept that authors discussed limitations carefully. Complete agreement that caveats are warranted and well-articulated.

OpenEval emphasizes widespread interactions and in vivo validation, while peer reviewers affirm support for epigenetic embedding theory and influence on environmental responses. Strong agreement on major implications.

Peer reviewers emphasize the dataset as a key community resource for functional interpretation. Strong agreement on broader impact and future directions.
